cases.caseName: Spinedex Physical Therapy USA Inc. v. United Healthcare of Arizona, Inc.
cases.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.precedentialStatus: Published — binding within the Ninth Circuit on the issues decided
cases.proceduralPosture: Appeal from summary judgment in an ERISA benefits action brought by a healthcare provider as assignee and would-be assignee.
cases.disposition: Reversed in part, affirmed in part, vacated in part, and remanded.
cases.holdingSummary: The court held that the provider had Article III standing as assignee to pursue assigned benefit-payment claims, while also holding that the assignment did not transfer fiduciary-duty claims and that one plan's anti-assignment clause barred assignment.
cases.materialFacts: A physical therapy provider sought payment of denied ERISA benefit claims assigned by patients. The plans and assignment language varied.
cases.relevance: Useful when reviewing provider standing, assignment language, plan-specific anti-assignment provisions, and exhaustion in reimbursement disputes.
cases.limitations: This was an ERISA denied-benefits case, not a ruling on Medicaid clawbacks, documentation sufficiency, or the merits of a particular overpayment demand. Outcomes depended on plan and assignment language.

cases.court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
cases.precedentialStatus: Published — binding within the Ninth Circuit on the issues decided
cases.proceduralPosture: Appeal after a bench-trial judgment and class certification in ERISA fiduciary-duty and denial-of-benefits litigation.
cases.disposition: Affirmed in part, reversed in part, and remanded.
cases.holdingSummary: The court upheld standing and fiduciary-duty class certification, but reversed denial-of-benefits class certification and the denial-of-benefits judgment; it also remanded an exhaustion issue affecting the fiduciary-duty claim.
cases.materialFacts: Plan beneficiaries challenged behavioral-health coverage guidelines used across multiple ERISA plans, alleging inconsistency with plan terms and certain state-mandated criteria.
cases.relevance: Useful for understanding how plan terms, internal clinical guidelines, class scope, and exhaustion can shape challenges to behavioral-health coverage decisions.
cases.limitations: This was a benefits-denial class action, not a provider reimbursement clawback decision. The appellate result was mixed and does not establish that any current payer guideline or audit finding is invalid.
